paper.title: Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?
paper.code_data_availability: "Information concerning access to the data used in this paper is available as supplemental material online." (p. 1136). The paper uses Danish administrative register data; no DST project number is given in the article text.

registers.name_in_paper: Data on the payout of parental leave benefits to individuals and the payout of leave reimbursements to firms
registers.role: treatment / outcome (parental leave days, paid vs unpaid leave)
linkage / outcomes (employment stock, turnover, new hires) / controls (labor market experience)

registers.name_in_paper: Oplysningssedler (yearly administrative data on wage payments from firms to workers)
variables_mentioned: total pretax payments from the main job

registers.role: outcomes (approximate hours of work, scaled to full-time equivalents)
outcomes (firm sales, purchases, gross profits proxy, firm survival)

registers.name_in_paper: Data on take-up of publicly paid sick days

linkages: Individual worker fertility and leave-taking linked to full administrative data on the employing firm and on coworkers
Workers linked to firms through matched employer-employee data (IDA 'main November employment relationship')
Children linked to mothers through parent-child linkages in the Central Person Registry to construct fertility histories
Coworkers linked to the treatment/control woman through joint employment at the baseline firm in the baseline year

sample.universe: The universe of Danish firms and workers, 2001-2013; births to prime-age women in Denmark 2003-2012 (504,810 births to prime-age women over the sample period)
sample.unit_of_observation: Event-firm-year (an event is a woman-firm-baseline-year combination) for firm outcomes; coworker-year for coworker outcomes
selection_rules: Potential events are woman-firm-year combinations in which a woman had her main job at some firm in some year; the baseline year is that year and the event year is 2 years later
Treatment event: the woman gives birth in the event year but not in the year before or after
Control event: the woman does not give birth in the event year, the year prior, or the year after
The woman must be of prime childbearing age, between 19 and 33 in the baseline year
The woman must have tenure at her baseline firm of at least a year and not be a student
The firm must employ a stock of between three and 30 employees in the baseline year
The firm must be in the private sector
The firm must be active at baseline on the basis of sales, hours and the total wage bill
The firm must not be an extreme outlier in terms of growth, sales levels or wage bill
Exact matching on the table 2 baseline observables; control events reweighted by 1/K
Trimming following Crump et al. (2009): cells with a control fraction above 0.9 or below 0.1 are discarded

Coworker sample: all male and female coworkers of the treatment/control woman in the baseline year whose job at the baseline firm is their main labor-market attachment and who had hours of at least half a full-time employee and earnings exceeding 75,000 DKK in the baseline year
When estimating equation (1), only events with data available for all 7 years (t = -4 to t = 2) are included
sample.n_observations: Firm sample: 31,908 observations (19,868 weighted), 16,080 firm clusters. Coworker sample: 268,403 observations at t = 0 and 267,213 at t = 1. No replacement firm subsample: 3,191 observations (2,010 weighted), 2,718 firm clusters.
sample.n_individuals: 9,934 treatment events and 9,934 (reweighted) control events after matching, covering 16,080 unique firms; before trimming, 23,734 treatment and 155,625 control events covering 44,165 unique firms

construction_notes: Hours are an approximation built from firms' mandatory ATP pension contributions, scaled so that hours are measured in full-time equivalent (FTE) workers; because contributions follow a stepwise function the measure misses overtime and small changes in existing employees' hours
The employee stock uses IDA's 'main November employment relationship' definition and includes workers on leave

The firm-level total wage bill is the sum of all (pretax) payments to workers during the year and includes payments to workers on paid parental leave; a second measure, the wage bill excluding leave, removes those payments
Total variable costs are approximated by adding firms' total purchases (VAT data) to the wage bill excluding leave
Gross profits are proxied by total sales minus purchases minus the total wage bill excluding leave; this differs from the accounting definition because VAT purchase data include capital equipment
Firms that are inactive and/or shut down are not removed; they are treated as having zero employees, zero hours and zero sales, and positive sales is used as a proxy for firm activity
The parental leave measure covers paid and unpaid leave and includes instances where the leave period is extended because of pregnancy-related health issues
Outlier firms are those with sales per employee below 10,000 DKK or above 100 million DKK and firms with wages per worker below 10,000 DKK or above 1 million DKK
For earnings and sales, matching quintiles are computed separately for each year to account for inflation; quintiles are computed on the analysis sample rather than the population
Standard errors are clustered at the firm level because parental leave is a firm-wide event
A woman or firm may enter the sample more than once as part of different events; a majority of firms enter only once

claims.statement: Having one additional employee give birth and go on parental leave increases parental leave days at firm, among small private Danish firms, measured in the event year (t = 0).

treatment.label: Number of births at the firm in the event year (BirthsInEventYear), instrumented by treatment status

register_source.value: Central Person Registry: parent-child linkages and birth dates, used to construct fertility histories

definition.value: BirthsInEventYear_ef, the total number of births among the firm's employees in the event year, instrumented with Treatment_e, an indicator for the event being a treatment event (a woman employed at the firm in the baseline year gives birth in the event year and not in the year before or after). The event year is 2 years after the baseline year.

timing.value: Measured in the event year (t = 0); outcomes are differenced from the baseline year t = -2

register_source.value: Data on the payout of parental leave benefits to individuals and the payout of leave reimbursements to firms (register not named by the paper)

definition.value: Total number of days of parental leave at the firm during the year, calculated from the payout of parental leave benefits to individuals and of leave reimbursements to firms; covers both paid and unpaid leave and includes extensions due to pregnancy-related health issues. Entered as the change from the baseline year t = -2.

timing.value: event year (t = 0), outcome differenced from the baseline year t = -2

units.value: days of parental leave at the firm per one additional birth at the firm in the event year

magnitude.interpretation: When we take these preferred specifications into account, one additional female employee giving birth in the event year leads to an increase in total leave days at the firm of 196 in the event year (col. 1) and 86 in the following year (col. 2).

estimand.target_population: Firms with 3-30 employees in the private sector in Denmark that employ a woman aged 19-33 at baseline with at least 1 year of tenure and who is not a student; treatment events are those where the woman gives birth in the event year (and not in the adjacent years), control events those where she does not give birth in the event year, the year before or the year after
estimand.compliers: Firms where the woman employed at baseline is still with the firm in the event year, so that her birth translates into an additional birth (and parental leave) at that firm; the fraction of potential mothers still with the treatment firm in the event year is 0.62 in the raw data
estimand.time_horizon: Effect in the event year (the calendar year of the birth)
estimand.formal_query: E[DeltaY | do(BirthsInEventYear = b+1)] - E[DeltaY | do(BirthsInEventYear = b)] for compliers

population.description: Matched and reweighted treatment and control events (woman-firm-baseline-year combinations) at small private Danish firms; firm-level data
population.ages: Woman aged 19-33 in the baseline year
population.period: Baseline years such that births occur 2003-2012; register data 2001-2013
subgroups_defined: No replacement firms (no other employee in the woman's one-digit occupation at baseline)
population.selection: Events are woman-firm-baseline-year combinations. The woman must be 19-33 in the baseline year, have at least 1 year of tenure at her baseline firm and not be a student; the firm must be private, active at baseline on sales, hours and wage bill, employ a stock of 3-30 employees, and not be an extreme outlier in growth, sales levels or wage bill. Treatment events are births in the event year with no birth in the adjacent years; control events have no birth in the event year, the year prior or the year after. Cells are exact-matched on the table 2 observables, controls reweighted 1/K, and cells with a control share above 0.9 or below 0.1 trimmed (Crump et al. 2009).

identification.source_of_variation: The timing of a female employee's first observed birth: treatment events are woman-firm-baseline-year combinations in which the woman gives birth in the event year (2 years after the baseline year) and not in the adjacent years, matched to observationally equivalent control events in which she does not give birth in the event year, the year before or the year after. Treatment status instruments the number of births at the firm in the event year.
identification.instrument: Treatment_e, an indicator for the event being a treatment event

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: 2 years prior to their eventual birth, treatment women are not sorted into firms that evolve along systematically different time trends than the firms of control women
key_assumptions.supported_by: Matching and reweighting on the table 2 baseline observables; pretrend tests showing the event-study estimates at t = -4 and t = -3 are not statistically significantly different from zero; balance on baseline observables not used in matching (table A3) and on industry composition (fig. A1)

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: a birth to a female employee working at firm f at baseline increases the probability of a birth in the event year at firm f
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption in sec. V.E; not separately tested

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: treatment status shifts the number of births at the firm in the event year
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage F-statistics reported for every panel and column; figure 3A shows treatment firms experience 0.68 additional births in the event year

implies_edges.to: Number of births at the firm in the event year

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: treatment status affects the firm and coworker outcomes only through births (and the resulting parental leave) at the firm in the event year
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not separately tested; sec. VI.H argues that other labor supply changes around childbirth are an order of magnitude smaller than the direct leave absence

implies_edges.to: Parental leave days at firm

key_assumptions.assumption: Common support: for each combination of the matching observables there are both treatment and control events
key_assumptions.supported_by: Trimming following Crump et al. (2009), discarding cells where the fraction of control observations exceeds 0.9 or falls below 0.1

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on the sample restrictions and on lying in a common-support exact-matching cell
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sec. V.B sample restrictions and sec. V.F matching, reweighting and trimming; table 3 documents the resulting selection

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion in the matched, reweighted and trimmed analysis sample
implies_edges.to: Parental leave days at firm

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation in the baseline year: the baseline year t = -2 is unaffected by the eventual birth (the year before the birth is already treated as potentially treated)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sec. V.C treats the coefficient at t = -1 as capturing anticipation effects; the pretrend coefficients at t = -4 and t = -3 are statistically indistinguishable from zero

implies_edges.to: Outcome in the baseline year t = -2

threats_discussed: Women who later give birth could choose to work at particularly family-friendly firms already before becoming pregnant, leading to differences between the groups of firms employing treatment and control women
A woman could endogenously time her fertility, resulting in correlations of firm trends with the timing of her fertility
Imperfect compliance: women employed at the baseline firm may leave before the event year, so treatment firms may not experience their worker's childbirth
The estimates may reflect other labor supply changes around childbirth rather than the parental leave absence itself (sec. VI.H)
The hours measure, built from stepwise ATP pension contributions, does not capture overtime or smaller changes in weekly hours and may understate hours increases
The gross profits proxy is noisy and departs from the standard accounting definition because VAT purchase data include capital equipment
Trimming for common support entails a potential loss of external validity and sample size
robustness_checks: Pretrend tests: difference-in-differences estimates at event times t = -4 and t = -3 are not statistically significantly different from zero
Balance of treatment and (reweighted) control samples on baseline observables not used in matching (table A3) and on industry composition (fig. A1)
OLS specifications with controls for baseline characteristics instead of matching and reweighting (app. G)
A coarser matching and reweighting procedure that trims fewer observations (app. H)
Comparison of the analysis sample with the universe of private sector firms (app. I)
Firms' purchases used as an identification check
Table A4: full-sample 2SLS with the main effect and instrument interacted with a no replacement firm indicator
Appendix K: direct comparison of the magnitude of parental leave absence with other labor supply adjustments around childbirth
Appendix L: heterogeneity by firm size
unresolved_confounders: By construction the design identifies the joint effect of the woman going on parental leave and any other labor supply changes occurring around childbirth; the authors argue, but cannot directly verify, that the latter are an order of magnitude smaller
The approximate FTE hours measure may be a lower bound on the true increase in hours because it misses overtime and small weekly-hours changes

estimator.value: 2SLS (two-stage least squares) on the first-differenced specification (2)-(3), estimated on the matched and reweighted sample

estimation.specification: Equation (3): the change in the outcome between the event year (col. 1) and the baseline year t = -2 is regressed on the number of births at the firm in the event year, instrumented by treatment status. First-stage F-statistic for this panel at t = 0 / t = 1: 2,194 / 2,194.
controls: Exact matching and reweighting on the baseline observables listed in table 2 (implemented through the sample and weights rather than as regressors)
estimation.weights: Control events reweighted by 1/K within exact-matching cells, where K is the number of control events matched to a treatment event

source_table.value: Table 5, panel A. Firm Outcomes, row 'Parental leave days at firm', col (1)

adjustment_set.label: Indicator for the woman having at least 2 years of tenure with the firm
Quintiles of the firm's number of employees
Quintiles of the share of female employees at the firm
Quintiles of the average number of children per employee

heterogeneity.dimension: Firms with versus without another employee in the same one-digit occupation as the woman on leave ('no replacement firms', 10% of the main sample)
heterogeneity.finding: For no replacement firms the paper estimates negative effects on total hours and on the wage bill excluding paid leave in the event year, unlike in the overall sample (table 9).

heterogeneity.dimension: Firm size
heterogeneity.finding: Appendix L sees no indications that the effects of parental leave vary with firm size, but standard errors are fairly wide.

population.selection: Events are woman-firm-baseline-year combinations. identification.source_of_variation: The timing of a female employee's first observed birth: treatment events are woman-firm-baseline-year combinations in which the woman gives birth in the event year (2 years after the baseline year) and not in the adjacent years, matched to observationally equivalent control events in which she does not give birth in the event year, the year before or the year after. Treatment status instruments the number of births at the firm in the event year.

claims.statement: Having 1% of the baseline workforce give birth and go on parental leave has no statistically significant effect on any sick days, among same-occupation coworkers, measured in the event year (t = 0).

timing.value: Measured in the event year (t = 0); outcomes are differenced from the baseline year t = -2

population.description: Baseline-year coworkers who are in the same one-digit occupation as the woman on leave
population.period: Baseline years such that births occur 2003-2012; register data 2001-2013
subgroups_defined: No replacement firms (no other employee in the woman's one-digit occupation at baseline)
population.selection: Events are woman-firm-baseline-year combinations. The woman must be 19-33 in the baseline year, have at least 1 year of tenure at her baseline firm and not be a student; the firm must be private, active at baseline on sales, hours and wage bill, employ a stock of 3-30 employees, and not be an extreme outlier in growth, sales levels or wage bill. Treatment events are births in the event year with no birth in the adjacent years; control events have no birth in the event year, the year prior or the year after. Cells are exact-matched on the table 2 observables, controls reweighted 1/K, and cells with a control share above 0.9 or below 0.1 trimmed (Crump et al. 2009).

identification.source_of_variation: The timing of a female employee's first observed birth: treatment events are woman-firm-baseline-year combinations in which the woman gives birth in the event year (2 years after the baseline year) and not in the adjacent years, matched to observationally equivalent control events in which she does not give birth in the event year, the year before or the year after. Treatment status instruments the number of births at the firm in the event year.

A woman could endogenously time her fertility, resulting in correlations of firm trends with the timing of her fertility
Imperfect compliance: women employed at the baseline firm may leave before the event year, so treatment firms may not experience their worker's childbirth
The estimates may reflect other labor supply changes around childbirth rather than the parental leave absence itself (sec. VI.H)
The hours measure, built from stepwise ATP pension contributions, does not capture overtime or smaller changes in weekly hours and may understate hours increases
The gross profits proxy is noisy and departs from the standard accounting definition because VAT purchase data include capital equipment
Trimming for common support entails a potential loss of external validity and sample size

ambiguities: The point estimate is the magnitude the authors state in the text for the plotted OLS coefficient; the figure itself prints no numerical value, and no standard error is reported for it.

evidence.annotation: FIG. 3.-Estimates for firms' total births and parental leave days (OLS). A and B show difference-in-differences estimates. Circles and solid lines show the estimated difference between the treatment and control firms from 4 years prior to the event year until 2 years after. The baseline year is 2 years prior to the event year, implying that the difference is identically zero here. Dashed lines show the 95% confidence interval based on standard errors clustered at the firm level. For comparison, C and D show sample means over time.

evidence.how: The figure plots the point estimates with 95% confidence bands; the paper states the magnitudes in the text but prints no standard error, confidence-interval endpoints or p-value for this coefficient.
The figure draws dashed 95% confidence bands but prints no numerical interval endpoints for this coefficient.

value.as_printed:
Y_eft = gamma_e + sum_{k in T} alpha_k 1_{t=k} + sum_{k in T} beta_k 1_{t=k} x Treatment_e + epsilon_eft,   (1)
T = {-4, -3, -1, 0, 1, 2}.
value.lhs: Y_eft (firm outcome for firm f at event time t)

terms.expression: sum_{k in T} beta_k 1_{t=k} x Treatment_e

value.normalisation: Event time t = -2 (the baseline year) is the omitted category, so the treatment-control difference is identically zero there; gamma_e is an event fixed effect absorbing baseline level differences.

falsification.condition: The identifying parallel-trends assumption would be rejected if the difference-in-differences estimates at event times t = -4 and t = -3 were statistically significantly different from zero; the paper states that its design passes these pretrends tests.
